To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the presence of glucose, sucrose, fructose and meat extract in the anaerobic digestion process induced the degradation of sulfamethazin (SMZ), a veterinary antibiotic.
sucrose, glucose, ethanol, fructose and meat extract exert an inducing effect on sulfamethazine removal by anaerobically digested sludge.
sucrose, glucose, and meat extract exert an inducing effect on sulfamethazine degradation in anaerobic sludges.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the stages of anaerbic digestion involved in the bioremediation of SMZ.
the identification of the microbial groups involved in the cometabolism of SMZ and the organic carbon substrates that induce this process.

the identification of the stages of anaerbic digestion potentially involved in SMZ biodegradation and the evaluation of the contribution of selected carbon sources to the cometabolism of this antimicrobial.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SMZ cometabolic degradation is associated with the degradation of soluble organic substrates, but the specific microbial groups responsible for SMZ removal remain to be identified.
the anaerobic degradation of sulfamethazin is a complex process, which is likely to occur via cometabolic and abiotic pathways.
the cometabolism of SMZ is likely to be associated to a particular microbial group, which is able to degrade the organic substrates fructose, glucose, sucrose and/or meat extract.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anaerobic cometabolic degradation of SMZ is not associated to any of the selected organic substrates, and that SMZ degradation occurs at the level of the microbial consortium.
SMZ cometabolic removal by anaerobically digesting sludge is associated with organic substrates that are not readily degraded in anaerobic digestion.
the cometabolism of SMZ is likely to occur during the hydrolytic phase, but the exact mechanism of this cometabolism is still not clear and needs to be further studied.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cometabolic removal of SMZ in the presence of organic substrates is likely to be due to the action of particular microbial groups, which are not involved in the anaerobic degradation of the substrates.
the cometabolic degradation of SMZ can occur during the degradation of different organic substrates.
SMZ degradation is not limited to a specific group of bacteria but can be achieved by a range of different microbial groups.
